title: why it's said three times
hook: om shanti shanti shanti: three times, never once, and there's a reason
tomorrow: why Indian kids touch their grandparents' feet

segments.voice: Yesterday: dharma, what holds things up. Today, a word you've probably heard said three times in a row.

Om shanti shanti shanti. It closes a lot of Hindu prayers, and more than a few yoga classes. Not once, not twice: three times. That isn't just for the rhythm. Traditional teachers read the three as a list. First, a guess at the word.

Shanti means peace, the settled kind: calm water with nothing stirring it. The Bhagavad Gita puts it bluntly: for someone without peace, how can there be happiness? Now the three. Traditional teachers read the three shantis as three kinds of trouble, the three places a bad day can come from. Trouble from forces beyond anyone's control: storms, floods, the world. Trouble from other beings: the friend who didn't call, the driver who cut in. And trouble from within: your own body and your own mind. Three sources, three shantis. The teachers add something practical. There's little anyone can do about the first, more about the second, and the third is the one most within reach, and the easiest to skip. So the chant isn't padding. It goes down the list: peace out there, peace between us, peace in here.
screen: `SHANTI — THE SETTLED KIND.` · `THE WORLD.` · `OTHER PEOPLE.` · `YOUR OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell, one shanti on each, said silently. First out-breath: toward the world. Second: toward one person you're not at peace with. You don't have to forgive them. Third: toward your own mind.
Shanti. Peace, the settled kind, said three times: the world, other people, your own mind. Fourth word.
Your line: peace, peace, peace. Next time something rattles you, there are three places it could have come from. That's day four.

howItsDone: Hindu prayers, readings and ceremonies often close with om shanti shanti shanti, the word for peace said three times.

myth: shanti is said three times just for the rhythm
traditional teachers read the three as three sources of trouble: the world, others, and yourself.
the Gita asks how someone without peace can be happy
Bhagavad Gita 2.66: without peace, how can there be happiness?

fork.setup: someone cuts you off in traffic. then you replay it in your head for the next hour. which shanti does the hour of replay need?
fork.reveal: the driver was other people. the hour of replay is the third, your own mind, the one that's most within reach.

original.note: Sanskrit: peace, calm, quiet. said three times at the close of the peace chants.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm word to end on.
what it means: peace in three directions: the world, other people, your own mind.
what a scholar hears: the Samkhya Karika opens with threefold suffering; commentators name it from within (adhyatmika), from other beings (adhibhautika) and from forces beyond (adhidaivika).

story.title: before the lesson began
story.text: In the old forest schools, a lesson didn't start with the lesson. Teacher and student first said a prayer together, and it's still chanted today. May we both be protected. May we both be nourished. May we work together with strength. May what we study shine. May we never turn against each other. And then, at the end: om shanti shanti shanti. Before a single word was taught, both of them asked for peace in all three directions.
story.source: the peace chant saha navavatu (Katha and Taittiriya Upanishads)

think.setup: a storm delays your flight. you snap at the gate agent, then replay it all evening. which part was most within reach?
think.reveal: the storm was the world, the agent was another person. the replay is the third shanti, your own mind, the one most within reach.

notes: Samkhya Karika 1 names threefold suffering (duhkha-traya); the division into adhyatmika, adhibhautika and adhidaivika comes from the commentaries (e.g. Gaudapada). The script says 'some teachers read the three shantis against that list'; confirm the attribution and that the pairing with the three shantis is a fair traditional reading.

Hook says om shanti shanti shanti 'closes the peace chants that open the Upanishads'; confirm phrasing (the shanti patha attached to the principal Upanishads). 'Some of the oldest Hindu texts' was cut as a superlative.

Cut from manuscript day 4 under the claims rule: 'the ancient texts, which are otherwise extremely economical with words', 'one of the most practical ideas in the whole tradition', 'the thing you said in 2019', and 'the ending of every prayer, every class, every text'.
Audit pass: adhidaivika is literally trouble from the devas; the teach now says the commentators tie it to the gods and the elements, so 'forces beyond anyone's control' is not a bare modern gloss.

Editor pass: 'illness' moved out of the first shanti (bodily illness belongs to adhyatmika, trouble from within, in the commentaries) and replaced with storms and floods; 'an aching back' added to the third; 'the replay at two in the morning' trimmed (late-night image echoed day 1) and 'the sentence you said' made impersonal; 'you'll start sorting your own day' (predicting the listener) softened; the within-reach point now attributed to teachers who use the list.
